52.11881,-106.66332: Marr Residence Built in 1884 by the Marr family, the Marr Residence is the oldest building in Saskatoon on its original location and one of the first to be built in the settlement. During the Rebellion of 1885 the residence served as a field hospital for the Canadian militia. Eighty-five wounded men arrived from Batoche by river on the steamer Northcote and were treated in this and two adjoining houses in May and June of 1885. Notable features of the house are its mansard roof and dormer windows. The City of Saskatoon purchased the property in 1979 and restored the house during 1983-84 in co-operation with Meewasin and the Province of Saskatchewan.
52.12919,-106.63788: Rugby Chapel 1912 The gift of the students and staff of Rugby School, England, Rugby Chapel was erected by the students of Emmanuel College under the leadership of George Exton Lloyd, M. A., Principal, 1908-1916. Rugby Chapel replaced an earlier chapel, built in 1909, and served as the chapel of Emmanuel College until the erection of the Chapel of St. Chad in 1966. Memorials within the chapel record the service of pioneer workers and of men who gave their lives in the two World Wars. In aeternum domine verbum tuum permanet.
52.13158,-106.66993: Fairbanks-Morse Warehouse Constructed in 1911, the Fairbanks-Morse Warehouse was designed by Brown and Vallance, the firm which designed all the early University buildings. The façade is a handsome example of pre-World War I warehouse architecture. The building is closely associated with the business, political and cultural history of Saskatoon. Its first occupant, the Canadian Fairbanks-Morse Company Limited, was part of Saskatoon's rapid growth as a distribution centre for central Saskatchewan. By 1948, the building was home to the co-operative movement and housed a union hall and the local Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.) headquarters. In 2006, the exterior of the building was rehabilitated and the upper floors were converted to residential condominiums. The Fairbanks-Morse Warehouse was designated as Municipal Heritage Property on December 9, 1985.
52.13292,-106.62801: Dr Henry Taube Dr. Henry Taube received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1983. His Nobel Citation reads "for his studies of the mechanisms of electron transfer reactions particularly of metal complexes" It was said that his work "dominated the development of his subject both theoretically and experimentally, making 18 major discoveries." Dr. Taube was born in Neudorf, Saskatchewan and received his B.Sc. (1935) and his M.Sc. (1937) from the University of Saskatchewan. In 1940 he completed his Ph.D. at the University of California (Berkeley). In his acceptance speech, Dr. Taube said, "But the benefits of science are not to be reckoned only in terms of the physical. Science as in intellectual exercise enriches our culture and is in itself ennobling. Each new insight into how the atoms in their interactions express themselves in structure and transformations, not only of inanimate matter, but particularly also of living matter, provides a thrill."
52.15692,-106.58266: Forestry Farm Superintendent's Residence When the Sutherland Forest Nursery Station was established in 1913, this imposing brick house was built as the Superintendent's residence and office. It was home to two superintendents, James McLean (1914-1942) and William Leslie 'Les' Kerr (1942-1966). The house saw many distinguished visitors, who enjoyed the increasingly luxurious landscape of the park. During its operation, 1914-1965, the Nursery Station distributed some 147 million trees across the Central and Northern Prairies for use in farm shelterbelts. Through the dedicated efforts of the Friends of the Forestry Farm House, the Forestry Farm Superintendent's Residence has been restored to the 1920's period. The Superintendent's Residence was designated a Municipal Heritage Property on July 23, 1990.
